options.A: greater accuracy over short horizons but more frequent upgrades and downgrades of issuers.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 184 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Incorrect. A rating is an ordinal ranking of relative creditworthiness, not a cardinal probability of default, and by construction it is not a point-in-time measure.
explanations.C: Correct. A through-the-cycle rating deliberately looks past temporary, cyclical swings in a borrower's condition, so it migrates less often. That stability is bought at the cost of timeliness: the rating lags a genuine deterioration in near-term default risk.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Reacting quickly to current conditions, and so migrating often, describes a point-in-time approach such as a credit score. Through-the-cycle ratings trade exactly that responsiveness away in exchange for stability.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: An investor buys five-year protection on a single-name CDS referencing a corporate issuer. The investor's position is most likely equivalent to:

options.A: a short position in the credit risk of the reference entity, gaining if its credit quality deteriorates.
options.B: a long position in the credit risk of the reference entity, gaining if its credit quality improves further.
options.C: a long position in the reference entity's bond financed at the benchmark rate, carrying no credit exposure.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 185 | Fixed Income

explanations.A: Correct. The protection buyer pays a periodic premium and is compensated if a credit event occurs, so the position gains when the reference entity's credit spread widens. That is economically the same as being short the entity's bonds.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That is the protection seller's position. The seller receives the premium, is exposed to the credit and gains as spreads tighten, much as an investor who owns the bond does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A financed long bond position replicates the protection seller rather than the buyer, and it plainly does carry credit exposure; the protection buyer's exposure runs the other way.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: An investor has sold protection on a CDS index of 125 equally weighted investment-grade issuers. One of the reference entities experiences a credit event. The most likely consequence for the contract is that:

options.B: the whole index contract terminates and the investor settles on the full notional of its position.
options.C: the contract continues on the full notional, because the index coupon was standardised at inception.
options.A: the defaulted name is settled on 1/125 of the notional and the index continues on a reduced notional.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 186 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Incorrect. Termination and settlement on the full notional is what happens to a single-name CDS after its reference entity defaults. An index is built to survive individual defaults precisely so that it remains a tradable benchmark.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The coupon is indeed standardised, but that fixes the premium rate, not the notional. The notional is written down by the defaulted entity's weight, so subsequent premium payments fall.
explanations.A: Correct. An index CDS is a portfolio of equally weighted single-name exposures. A credit event settles only the defaulting name's share of the notional; that name is then removed and the contract runs on with the remaining names on a proportionately smaller notional.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: Following a possible credit event on a reference entity, the settlement of the outstanding CDS contracts is most likely determined by:

options.B: an ISDA determinations committee, with the recovery rate then fixed by an auction of the obligations.
options.C: each protection buyer separately, who must deliver the cheapest bond that it holds to the counterparty.
options.A: the rating agency that downgraded the entity, whose published recovery estimate sets the cash payment.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 187 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Correct. A regional ISDA determinations committee rules on whether a credit event has occurred and whether an auction will be held. The auction establishes a single market recovery price, allowing the great majority of contracts to settle in cash for (1 - recovery) x notional.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That is physical settlement, which still exists but is now the exception. The auction mechanism was introduced because the notional of CDS outstanding can far exceed the supply of deliverable bonds.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A downgrade is not a credit event, and rating agencies have no role in CDS settlement. The credit events recognised are bankruptcy, failure to pay and restructuring.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A five-year CDS on $10 million notional references a high-yield issuer. The CDS spread on the issuer is 450 bp, the contract's standardised coupon is 500 bp, and its effective spread duration is 4.0. The upfront payment on the contract is most likely:

options.B: $200,000 paid by the protection buyer to the protection seller.
options.C: $200,000 paid by the protection seller to the protection buyer.
options.A: $50,000 paid by the protection seller to the protection buyer.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 188 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Incorrect. The direction is reversed. The buyer pays an upfront amount only when the CDS spread exceeds the standardised coupon, so that the fixed coupon on its own would undercompensate the seller for the credit risk taken.
explanations.C: Correct. The upfront premium is approximately (CDS spread - fixed coupon) x effective spread duration = (4.50% - 5.00%) x 4.0 = -2.00% of notional. The negative sign means the buyer, having contracted to pay a coupon above the fair spread, is compensated: 2.00% x $10 million = $200,000 received from the seller.
explanations.A: Incorrect. $50,000 applies the 50 bp annual difference between coupon and spread to the notional for one year only. The upfront payment capitalises that difference over the life of the contract, which is what multiplying by the spread duration of 4.0 achieves.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A corporate bond trades at a credit spread of 320 bp, while the five-year CDS on the same issuer trades at 260 bp, and an investor expects the two to converge. The trade that most likely exploits this is to:

options.C: buy the bond and buy CDS protection, capturing the 60 bp of negative basis as it converges.
options.A: short the bond and sell CDS protection, capturing the 60 bp of positive basis as it converges.
options.B: sell five-year protection and buy ten-year protection, a curve steepener on the same issuer.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 189 | Fixed Income

explanations.C: Correct. The basis is the CDS spread minus the bond's credit spread, here 260 - 320 = -60 bp, a negative basis. Buying the bond earns 320 bp while buying protection costs 260 bp, so 60 bp is locked in with the credit risk largely hedged, and it is realised as the basis converges to zero.
explanations.A: Incorrect. That is the positive-basis trade, used when the CDS spread is the wider of the two. Here protection is the cheaper way to take the credit view, so it should be bought rather than sold.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That is a curve trade rather than a basis trade: it expresses a view on the shape of the issuer's credit curve, gaining if long-dated spreads widen relative to short-dated ones, and is indifferent to the CDS-bond basis.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: In a securitisation, the true sale of the loan pool by the originator to a special purpose entity most likely allows the resulting ABS to:

options.C: dispense with credit tranching, because the true sale removes the pool's exposure to borrower default.
options.A: be rated on the credit quality of the pool alone, isolated from the originator's own bankruptcy.
options.B: be rated one notch below the originator, reflecting its continuing obligation to service the pool.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 190 | Fixed Income

explanations.C: Incorrect. A true sale addresses the seller's bankruptcy risk, not the borrowers' default risk. The pool's own credit losses remain and are handled by credit enhancement such as subordination, overcollateralisation and reserve accounts.
explanations.A: Correct. A true sale to a bankruptcy-remote SPE puts the collateral beyond the reach of the originator's creditors. Investors then bear the risk of the pool rather than of the seller, which is why an ABS can be rated above the entity that originated it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no fixed notching relationship to the originator; breaking that link is the whole purpose of the structure, and servicing can be transferred to a back-up servicer if the originator fails.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A securitisation issues Class A, Class B and Class C notes, with losses on the pool absorbed first by Class C, and it also splits Class A into A-1 and A-2 notes that are repaid in strict order. These two features are best described as:

options.C: credit tranching across A/B/C and time tranching within Class A.
options.A: time tranching across A/B/C and credit tranching within Class A.
options.B: credit tranching in both cases, since each reorders the waterfall.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 191 | Fixed Income

explanations.C: Correct. Credit tranching, or subordination, allocates losses in a set order so that the junior class absorbs them first. Time tranching allocates principal repayments in a set order, redistributing prepayment and extension risk without altering loss priority.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The two labels are the wrong way round. Absorbing losses in a set order is credit tranching; repaying principal sequentially is time tranching.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both features are implemented through the waterfall, but only the A/B/C subordination reorders losses. Sequential-pay A-1 and A-2 notes share the same loss priority and differ only in when principal reaches them.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A mortgage pass-through pool begins a month with an outstanding balance of $80,000,000. Scheduled principal repayment for that month is $250,000 and the single monthly mortality rate is 0.60%. The prepayment for the month is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 192 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Correct. The SMM is applied to the balance remaining after the scheduled principal payment: 0.0060 x ($80,000,000 - $250,000) = $478,500. SMM measures principal repaid in excess of the amortisation schedule, and its annualised counterpart is the CPR.
explanations.C: Incorrect. $480,000 applies the SMM to the full beginning balance without first deducting the scheduled principal. Scheduled amortisation is not a prepayment, so it must be taken out of the base first.
explanations.A: Incorrect. $728,500 is the total principal received for the month, being scheduled principal of $250,000 plus the prepayment. The prepayment is only the part in excess of the schedule.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A CMO contains a PAC tranche with an initial collar of 90 to 300 PSA and a single support tranche. Prepayments then run at 400 PSA for an extended period. The most likely result is that:

options.B: the support tranche is repaid faster, and once it is retired the PAC's schedule is no longer protected.
options.C: the PAC tranche is repaid faster, and the support tranche's average life is extended past its schedule.
options.A: both tranches are repaid faster in proportion to their balances, as they would be in a sequential-pay CMO.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 193 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Correct. The support tranche absorbs principal above the upper collar, so it shortens first while the PAC keeps to its schedule. As the support shrinks the PAC's effective collar narrows, and once the support is gone the PAC bears the contraction risk itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The direction of protection is reversed: the PAC is the protected class. Extension of the support tranche is what happens when prepayments run below the lower collar, not above the upper one.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither allocation described here happens. Principal is allocated by rule so as to hold the PAC on schedule, and a sequential-pay CMO retires its classes one after another rather than pro rata.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: During the lockout period of a credit card receivable ABS, the principal collected from the cardholders is most likely:

options.C: distributed to the noteholders in order of seniority, shortening the notes' average lives.
options.A: held in a reserve account until the notes amortise, which lowers the deal's overall yield.
options.B: used to buy further receivables from the originator, leaving the notes' principal outstanding.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 194 | Fixed Income

explanations.C: Incorrect. That describes the amortisation period after lockout, or an amortising deal such as an auto loan ABS, where scheduled principal and prepayments are passed through as they are collected.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Cash is reinvested in receivables rather than parked. A reserve account is a separately funded form of credit enhancement, and it is an early amortisation trigger, not a reserve, that protects investors if pool performance deteriorates.
explanations.B: Correct. A credit card ABS is a revolving structure. The underlying receivables turn over very quickly, so during the lockout period principal collections are reinvested in new receivables and investors receive interest only; principal is repaid in the amortisation period that follows.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A covered bond is best distinguished from an otherwise similar asset-backed security by the fact that:

options.B: the cover pool stays on the issuer's balance sheet and investors also have recourse to the issuer.
options.C: the cover pool is sold to a bankruptcy-remote entity and investors rank ahead of other creditors.
options.A: the cover pool is static, so assets in it that default or prepay are never replaced by the issuer.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 195 | Fixed Income

explanations.B: Correct. Covered bonds provide dual recourse: a claim on a segregated cover pool and an unsecured claim on the issuing institution itself. The assets are not derecognised, and the issuer must keep the pool sound, which is why covered bonds are usually rated above and yield less than a comparable ABS.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Selling the pool to a bankruptcy-remote SPE with no recourse to the seller is the ABS or CDO structure. A covered bond does the opposite, keeping the pool with the issuer and adding a claim on it.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The reverse is true: a cover pool is dynamic and must be maintained, with non-performing or prepaid assets replaced by the issuer. A static pool is more characteristic of an ABS.

subject: Fixed Income

stem: A stock trades at 50.00. The stock will pay a single dividend of 2.00 exactly one year from today, immediately before a one-year forward contract on it expires, and the one-year risk-free rate is 5.0% (annually compounded). The no-arbitrage forward price is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 196 | Derivatives

explanations.B: Correct. The carry-arbitrage model gives F0(T) = S0(1 + r)^T minus the future value of the carry benefits: 50.00(1.05) - 2.00 = 52.50 - 2.00 = 50.50. A dividend is a benefit the holder of the asset receives but the long of the forward does not, so it lowers the forward price.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 52.50 is S0(1 + r)^T, the forward price for an otherwise identical stock that pays no dividend. It charges the long for a cash flow he will never receive, and a trader could arbitrage it by buying the stock and selling the forward.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 50.40 is (50.00 - 2.00)(1.05), which subtracts the dividend from the spot price and then compounds. That treats the dividend as if it were paid today; because it is paid at expiration, only its future value of 2.00 is deducted.

subject: Derivatives

stem: Two years ago an investor took the long side of a three-year forward contract on a non-dividend-paying stock at a forward price of 105.00. The contract now has exactly one year remaining, the stock trades at 104.00, and the one-year risk-free rate is 5.0% (annually compounded). The value of the contract to the long is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 197 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. Valuing a forward during its life nets the spot price against the present value of the contracted forward price: Vt = St - F0/(1 + r)^(T - t) = 104.00 - 105.00/1.05 = 104.00 - 100.00 = 4.00.
explanations.B: Incorrect. -1.00 is simply St - F0. It sets today's stock price against a payment that is not due for another year, so the time value of the deferred forward price is ignored; the forward price must be discounted first.
explanations.C: Incorrect. -0.95 is (104.00 - 105.00)/1.05, discounting the whole difference. Only the forward price is deferred to expiration; the stock is already worth 104.00 today, so the spot leg is not discounted.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A 1 x 4 forward rate agreement on 90-day MRR with a notional of 10,000,000 was entered at a fixed rate of 4.00%. At the expiration of the FRA, 90-day MRR sets at 5.00%. The cash settlement received by the long (the fixed-rate payer) at that date is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 198 | Derivatives

explanations.C: Correct. The interest advantage is 10,000,000 x (0.0500 - 0.0400) x (90/360) = 25,000, but that advantage would only be realized 90 days later. An FRA settles at expiration, so the payment is discounted at the settlement rate: 25,000/(1 + 0.05 x 90/360) = 24,691.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 25,000 is the undiscounted differential that would accrue over the 90-day deposit period. Because the FRA pays at the start of that period rather than at its end, the amount must be brought back to present value.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 100,000 applies the 1.00% rate differential to the notional for a full year. The contract references a 90-day rate, so the differential must be scaled by the 90/360 day-count fraction before it is applied.

subject: Derivatives

stem: The spot exchange rate is 1.0200 USD per EUR. The one-year risk-free rate is 5.0% in USD and 2.0% in EUR, both annually compounded. Under covered interest rate parity, the one-year forward rate, quoted in USD per EUR, is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 199 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. F0 = S0 x (1 + r of the price currency)/(1 + r of the base currency) = 1.0200 x (1.05/1.02) = 1.0500. Borrowing EUR, converting at spot and investing in USD must earn exactly the forward rate, or a riskless profit would exist.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.9909 is 1.0200 x (1.02/1.05), which inverts the ratio and so treats EUR as the price currency. In USD-per-EUR terms it is the base currency rate that belongs in the denominator.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.0924 is 1.0200 x 1.05 x 1.02, compounding the spot rate at both interest rates. Covered interest rate parity depends on the ratio of the two growth factors, not their product; only the differential matters.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A bond futures contract expires in one year. The cheapest-to-deliver bond has a full price (clean price plus accrued interest) of 104.00 today, pays no coupon before the contract expires, and will have accrued interest of 2.00 at expiration. Its conversion factor is 0.80 and the one-year risk-free rate is 5.0% (annually compounded). The quoted futures price is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 200 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. Carry the full price forward, remove the accrued interest that will have built up at delivery, then adjust for the conversion factor: [104.00(1.05) - 2.00]/0.80 = 107.20/0.80 = 134.00.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 136.50 is 109.20/0.80, which omits the 2.00 of accrued interest. Futures prices are quoted on a clean basis, so accrued interest at the delivery date has to be stripped out of the carried-forward full price.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 85.76 is 107.20 x 0.80, multiplying by the conversion factor rather than dividing. The factor scales the invoice amount the short receives, so it enters the quoted futures price as a divisor.

subject: Derivatives

stem: The present value factors for annual payment dates one, two and three years from today are 0.96, 0.92 and 0.88 respectively. The fixed rate on a new three-year annual-pay interest rate swap settling on those dates is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 201 | Derivatives

explanations.B: Correct. The swap rate is the coupon that prices the fixed leg at par: (1 - the final discount factor)/(the sum of the discount factors) = (1 - 0.88)/(0.96 + 0.92 + 0.88) = 0.12/2.76 = 4.35%. At that rate the two legs have equal present value, so the swap is worth zero at inception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.00% is 0.12/3, dividing by the number of payment dates instead of by the sum of the discount factors. That would be right only if every factor equalled 1.00, that is, if money had no time value.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 1.45% is (1 - 0.96)/2.76, using the first-year factor in the numerator. The numerator must use the final-maturity factor, because the fixed leg is priced as a par bond redeeming on the last payment date.

subject: Derivatives

stem: An investor entered a three-year annual-pay interest rate swap as the fixed-rate payer at 4.00% on a notional of 10,000,000. One year later, with two payment dates remaining, the fixed rate on a new two-year swap is 5.00% and the present value factors for the two remaining dates are 0.95 and 0.90. The value of the existing swap to the fixed-rate payer is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 202 | Derivatives

explanations.C: Correct. Value to the payer = (new swap rate - contracted rate) x (sum of the remaining discount factors) x notional = (0.0500 - 0.0400) x (0.95 + 0.90) x 10,000,000 = 185,000. He is locked into paying 4.00% when the market now charges 5.00%, so the old contract is an asset.
explanations.A: Incorrect. -185,000 is the value of the identical swap to the fixed-rate receiver. Swap values are zero-sum between the counterparties, and when swap rates rise it is the payer who gains and the receiver who loses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 200,000 is 0.0100 x 2 x 10,000,000, adding the two annual savings of 100,000 without discounting them. Those savings arrive one and two years from now, so each must be multiplied by its present value factor.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A stock trades at 50.00. Over the next period it will rise to 60.00 with an actual probability of 0.70 or fall to 40.00 with an actual probability of 0.30. The per-period risk-free rate is 5.0%. A European call on the stock with an exercise price of 50.00 and one period to expiration is worth closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 203 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. The risk-neutral probability is (1 + r - d)/(u - d) = (1.05 - 0.80)/(1.20 - 0.80) = 0.625, and the call pays 10.00 up and 0 down, so the value is [0.625(10.00) + 0.375(0)]/1.05 = 6.25/1.05 = 5.95.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 6.25 is the risk-neutral expected payoff, 0.625 x 10.00, left undiscounted. That expectation is measured at expiration, so it must be brought back one period at the risk-free rate before it is a price today.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 6.67 is 0.70(10.00)/1.05, using the actual probability of an up move. Actual probabilities never enter, because the payoff can be replicated exactly with the stock and borrowing whatever an investor believes about them.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A stock trades at 40.00 and over one period will move to either 50.00 or 30.00. The per-period risk-free rate is 5.0%. The portfolio of stock and risk-free borrowing that replicates one European call with an exercise price of 44.00 and one period to expiration is best described as:

options.C: long 0.30 shares, financed by borrowing 8.57.
options.A: long 0.30 shares, financed by borrowing 9.00.
options.B: long 3.33 shares, financed by borrowing 8.57.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 204 | Derivatives

explanations.C: Correct. The hedge ratio is the spread in option values over the spread in stock values, (6.00 - 0)/(50.00 - 30.00) = 0.30. Borrowing is set so the portfolio pays nothing in the down state: 0.30(30.00)/1.05 = 8.57, which makes the call worth 0.30(40.00) - 8.57 = 3.43.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 9.00 is 0.30 x 30.00, the amount that must be repaid at expiration rather than the amount borrowed today. The loan proceeds are the present value of that repayment, 9.00/1.05 = 8.57.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 3.33 is 20.00/6.00, the hedge ratio turned upside down. The hedge ratio divides the spread in option values by the spread in stock values, so for a call it always falls between 0 and 1.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A stock trades at 100.00. In each of two periods it moves up by a factor of 1.20 or down by a factor of 0.80, and the risk-free rate is 4.0% per period. A European call with an exercise price of 100.00 and two periods to expiration is worth closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 205 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. The risk-neutral probability is (1.04 - 0.80)/(1.20 - 0.80) = 0.60. Only the up-up node finishes in the money, at 144.00 - 100.00 = 44.00, so the value is (0.60)^2(44.00)/(1.04)^2 = 15.84/1.0816 = 14.64.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 15.23 is 15.84/1.04, discounting the expected payoff over one period only. The payoff is received two periods from today, so the discounting must run over both periods.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 10.17 is (0.50)^2(44.00)/(1.04)^2, treating up and down moves as equally likely. The risk-neutral probability is pinned down by u, d and r, and here it works out to 0.60, not 0.50.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A dealer has written 5,000 call options, each on one share of the same stock. The Black-Scholes-Merton delta of the option is 0.60. The delta-neutral hedge for the dealer at this moment is best described as:

options.B: 3,000 shares held long.
options.C: 3,000 shares sold short.
options.A: 8,333 shares held long.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 206 | Derivatives

explanations.B: Correct. Each written call carries a delta of -0.60, so 5,000 of them amount to -3,000 share-equivalents. Buying 5,000 x 0.60 = 3,000 shares brings the position delta to zero; because delta itself then changes with the stock, the hedge has to be rebalanced.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Shorting 3,000 shares is the hedge for a long call position; here it would take the position to -6,000 deltas. A written call loses as the stock rises, so the offsetting position must be one that gains as the stock rises.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 8,333 is 5,000/0.60, dividing by delta instead of multiplying by it. Delta is the number of shares each option behaves like, so the share count is the number of options times delta, never the quotient.

subject: Derivatives

stem: The distinction between pricing a forward contract and valuing it is best described as follows: pricing determines the:

options.B: forward price at initiation, at which the contract is worth zero to both.
options.C: forward price at initiation, which equals the expected spot price at expiry.
options.A: contract's worth during its life, which changes as the spot price moves.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 207 | Derivatives

explanations.B: Correct. Pricing a forward means solving for the fixed rate written into the contract, and no-arbitrage sets that rate so that neither counterparty has to pay the other to enter. Valuation is the separate later question of what an existing contract has become worth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The no-arbitrage forward price is the spot price carried at the risk-free rate and adjusted for carry costs and benefits; it is not a forecast. It coincides with the expected future spot price only if investors are risk-neutral.
explanations.A: Incorrect. That describes valuation rather than pricing. The value of a forward is zero at initiation by construction and becomes non-zero afterwards as the spot price and the remaining time to expiration change.

subject: Derivatives

stem: In a bond futures contract under which the short may choose among several eligible bonds, the cheapest-to-deliver bond is best described as the eligible bond that:

options.C: minimizes the delivery cost net of the invoice amount the short receives.
options.A: carries the lowest conversion factor among the eligible deliverable bonds.
options.B: carries the lowest quoted market price among the eligible deliverable bonds.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 208 | Derivatives

explanations.C: Correct. For each eligible bond the short compares the cost of buying it with the invoice amount it earns, which is the futures settlement price times that bond's conversion factor plus accrued interest. The bond leaving the smallest net cost is cheapest to deliver.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The conversion factor exists to level out differences in coupon and maturity, so a low factor also scales down the invoice amount the short is paid. Taken on its own it says nothing about which bond is cheapest.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A cheap quoted price normally goes with a low conversion factor and hence a small invoice amount, and the two largely cancel. Cheapness has to be judged on the gap between purchase cost and invoice amount.

subject: Derivatives

stem: Two analysts value the same one-period European call with a binomial model. They agree on the stock price, the up and down factors, the exercise price and the risk-free rate, but disagree about the probability of an up move. Their computed call values are most likely:

options.C: identical, because the actual probability never enters the valuation.
options.A: identical, because the differing probabilities offset in the payoff.
options.B: different, because the expected payoff depends on the probabilities.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 209 | Derivatives

explanations.C: Correct. The call is valued by building a portfolio of the stock and risk-free borrowing that reproduces its payoff in both states. The cost of that portfolio depends only on the stock price, the up and down factors, the exercise price and the rate, so beliefs drop out.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Nothing offsets, because the actual probability is not used at all. The weights in the binomial formula are the risk-neutral probability (1 + r - d)/(u - d) and its complement, both derived from the tree and the risk-free rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That would hold if the option were valued as a real-world expected payoff discounted at a risk-adjusted rate. The replication argument sidesteps both the probabilities and the risk premium, which is exactly what makes the model workable.

subject: Derivatives

stem: In a binomial tree, the value of an American call on a stock that pays no dividends, relative to an otherwise identical European call, is most likely:

options.C: the same, because early exercise is never optimal at any node.
options.A: higher, because the right to exercise early always carries value.
options.B: lower, because exercising early forfeits the remaining time value.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 210 | Derivatives

explanations.C: Correct. At every node the value of continuing to hold exceeds the exercise value: exercising early surrenders the interest on the exercise price and the remaining optionality while capturing nothing, since there is no dividend. The early-exercise right is therefore never used.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The American feature can never be worth less than zero, but here it is worth exactly zero. It does add value for American puts, and for calls on a stock paying a dividend large enough to make early exercise worthwhile.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The holder of an American option is never forced to exercise and can always hold to expiration, so it can never be worth less than the European option. The extra right can only help, never hurt.

subject: Derivatives

stem: The Black-Scholes-Merton model assumes the underlying's continuously compounded returns are normally distributed with a constant, known volatility. The volatility skew routinely observed in equity index options is best interpreted as evidence that:

options.A: the return distribution has a fatter left tail than the model assumes.
options.B: the risk-free rate is not constant over the life of the options traded.
options.C: the underlying cannot be traded continuously without transaction costs.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 211 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. Implied volatility rises as the exercise price falls, meaning the market pays more for downside protection than a lognormal price distribution would justify. That is a statement about distributional shape: negative skew and excess weight in the left tail.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A shifting risk-free rate moves option values through rho, but it moves the whole surface at once. It cannot produce implied volatilities that differ systematically from one exercise price to the next.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transaction costs and discrete rebalancing do bias implied volatilities upward and cause hedging error, but they apply across the board. They do not explain why the bias concentrates at low exercise prices, which is what the skew describes.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A payer swaption is best described as an instrument that:

options.A: gives the holder the right to pay fixed on a swap, gaining value as rates rise.
options.B: gives the holder the right to receive fixed on a swap, gaining value as rates fall.
options.C: obliges the holder to pay fixed on a swap beginning at the expiration date.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 212 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. A payer swaption is the right, not the obligation, to enter a swap paying the pre-agreed fixed rate. It is exercised when the market swap rate at expiration is above that rate, so it gains as rates rise, the same directional exposure as an interest rate cap.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That describes a receiver swaption, the right to receive fixed and pay floating. It behaves like an interest rate floor and gains value when swap rates fall, the opposite exposure to a payer swaption.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A binding commitment to enter a swap on a future date at a set fixed rate is a forward swap, which costs nothing to enter. The premium paid for a swaption buys the right to walk away if rates move the wrong way.

subject: Derivatives

stem: A dealer maintains a delta-neutral hedge against a position in at-the-money call options with a short time to expiration. Gamma is best described as a measure that is:

options.A: largest near the money, showing how quickly the delta hedge goes stale.
options.B: largest deep in the money, showing the option's sensitivity to volatility.
options.C: constant across moneyness, showing the option's sensitivity to time decay.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 213 | Derivatives

explanations.A: Correct. Gamma is the rate of change of delta, and it peaks for at-the-money options close to expiration. High gamma means delta shifts sharply for a small move in the underlying, so a hedge that was neutral a moment ago is not, and rebalancing must be more frequent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gamma tends to zero both deep in and deep out of the money, where delta is already pinned near 1 or near 0 and barely moves. Sensitivity to volatility is vega, a separate Greek.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gamma varies sharply with both moneyness and time remaining, which is precisely why the hedging error grows with it. Sensitivity to the passage of time is theta, the change in option value as expiration nears.

subject: Derivatives

stem: An appraiser must value a recently completed, purpose-built research laboratory. The building is owner-occupied, no comparable laboratory has traded in the market, and no rental evidence for such space exists. The valuation approach the appraiser is most likely to rely on is best described as:

options.B: the sales comparison approach, since adjusting the prices of recent transactions is the most reliable route to market value.
options.C: the income approach, since capitalising the property's net operating income directly reflects an investor's required return.
options.A: the cost approach, since replacement cost less depreciation plus land value can be estimated without sales or rental evidence.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 214 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. The sales comparison approach adjusts the prices of recently transacted comparable properties, so it fails exactly where the stem places the appraiser: no comparable laboratory has traded. It is the preferred approach only in an active market with frequent, similar transactions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The income approach capitalises rental income and so requires observable market rents. An owner-occupied, purpose-built laboratory produces none, and inventing a hypothetical rent for a building with no rental market would drive the entire valuation.
explanations.A: Correct. The cost approach values the site and adds the depreciated replacement cost of the improvements, so it needs neither comparable sales nor market rents. It is the standard fallback for new, unusual or special-purpose buildings, and it also sets a practical ceiling on value, since a buyer would not pay more than the cost of building anew.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: In the direct capitalisation of a commercial property, net operating income is best described as effective gross income less:

options.C: operating expenses and depreciation, but before deducting income taxes, debt service and capital expenditures.
options.A: operating expenses, but before deducting depreciation, income taxes, debt service and capital expenditures.
options.B: operating expenses, depreciation and debt service, but before deducting income taxes and capital expenditures.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 215 | Alternative Investments

explanations.C: Incorrect. Depreciation is a non-cash accounting allocation, not a cash operating cost, and deducting it would understate the cash flow to which the capitalisation rate is applied. It belongs in an accounting income statement, not in an appraisal.
explanations.A: Correct. Net operating income is a pre-financing, pre-tax cash measure: effective gross income less cash operating expenses such as property taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs and management. Depreciation, income taxes, debt service and capital expenditures are all excluded, which is what makes the resulting capitalisation rate comparable across investors with different tax positions and financing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Debt service reflects how the buyer chose to finance the property, not the property's own earning power. Subtracting it produces the cash flow to equity, which is capitalised at an equity dividend rate rather than at a property capitalisation rate.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A commercial property has potential gross income of $2,000,000, a vacancy and collection loss allowance equal to 5% of potential gross income, and operating expenses of $700,000. An appraiser applies a going-in capitalisation rate of 8.0%. Using direct capitalisation, the indicated value of the property is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 216 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Correct. Effective gross income is $2,000,000 less the 5% vacancy allowance of $100,000, or $1,900,000. Net operating income is $1,900,000 - $700,000 = $1,200,000, and direct capitalisation gives $1,200,000 / 0.08 = $15,000,000.
explanations.C: Incorrect. $23,750,000 is effective gross income of $1,900,000 divided by 0.08, which omits the $700,000 of operating expenses. A capitalisation rate is derived from comparable sales as a ratio to net operating income, so it must be applied to net operating income.
explanations.A: Incorrect. $25,000,000 capitalises potential gross income of $2,000,000, ignoring both the vacancy allowance and operating expenses. No tenant-occupied property collects its full potential rent.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: An appraiser values an apartment building using the gross income multiplier method. A comparable building recently sold for $12,000,000 at a time when its effective gross income was $1,500,000. The subject building has potential gross income of $1,900,000, a vacancy allowance of $100,000 and operating expenses of $500,000. The indicated value of the subject building is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 217 | Alternative Investments

explanations.A: Incorrect. $10,400,000 applies the multiplier to income after deducting the $500,000 of operating expenses. The gross income multiplier is by construction a multiple of gross income; applying it to a net figure double-counts the expense deduction already embedded in the comparable's price.
explanations.B: Correct. The multiplier implied by the comparable is $12,000,000 / $1,500,000 = 8.0. The subject's effective gross income is $1,900,000 - $100,000 = $1,800,000, so the indicated value is 8.0 x $1,800,000 = $14,400,000. The method assumes the subject and the comparable share the same expense ratio, which is its principal weakness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. $15,200,000 applies the multiplier to potential gross income of $1,900,000. The comparable's multiplier was derived from effective gross income, so consistency requires it to be applied to the subject's effective gross income.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: In a discounted cash flow valuation of an office building, the terminal capitalisation rate applied to the net operating income of the year following the holding period is usually set above the going-in capitalisation rate. This is most likely because:

options.B: the terminal rate is applied to a nominal cash flow, so it must be grossed up for the inflation expected over the holding period.
options.C: the terminal value is discounted back to the present, so a higher rate is needed to offset the discounting of the resale proceeds.
options.A: the income being capitalised lies further in the future and is less certain, and the building will by then be older and less competitive.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 218 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. Capitalisation rates are already nominal, and the forecast terminal net operating income itself grows with inflation. Adjusting the rate as well as the cash flow would count inflation twice.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Discounting the resale proceeds to the present is a separate step, performed with the discount rate over the holding period. It has no bearing on the rate used to convert terminal income into a terminal value.
explanations.A: Correct. The exit capitalisation rate is applied to income forecast several years out, which carries much more forecast error, and it prices a building that will by then be older, closer to obsolescence and nearer to major capital spending. Both effects raise the yield a buyer at that future date would demand, so the exit rate normally exceeds the going-in rate.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: An investor buys a property for $10,000,000 that produces net operating income of $800,000. The purchase is financed with an interest-only loan at a loan-to-value ratio of 60% and an interest rate of 6.0%. The equity dividend rate on the investment is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 219 | Alternative Investments

explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.4% is $440,000 divided by the $10,000,000 total property value. The equity dividend rate is a cash-on-cash measure, so the denominator is the cash equity actually invested, not the whole purchase price.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 8.0% is the going-in capitalisation rate, $800,000 / $10,000,000. That is the unlevered return on the property before any debt service, and it is the benchmark against which leverage is judged.
explanations.B: Correct. Debt is 0.60 x $10,000,000 = $6,000,000, interest-only debt service is $360,000, and cash flow after debt service is $440,000 on $4,000,000 of equity, or 11.0%. Because the 8.0% capitalisation rate exceeds the 6.0% borrowing cost, leverage is positive and raises the equity return; the same figures give a debt service coverage ratio of $800,000 / $360,000 = 2.22.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: Compared with a real estate operating company (REOC), a REIT is most likely to:

options.B: retain a larger share of its earnings in order to fund development activity and property trading.
options.C: distribute most of its taxable income to shareholders in exchange for exemption from corporate income tax.
options.A: carry more leverage, because exemption from corporate income tax raises the value of the interest tax shield.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 220 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. Retaining earnings to fund development and trading describes a REOC, which is taxed as an ordinary corporation and faces no distribution requirement. That freedom is the main reason an operating company would choose not to elect REIT status.
explanations.C: Correct. A REIT obtains flow-through tax treatment by distributing the great majority of its taxable income, which is why REITs pay high dividends, retain little cash, and depend on issuing debt and equity to fund growth. A REOC pays corporate tax and can reinvest its cash flow instead.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The reasoning is inverted: a vehicle that already escapes corporate income tax gains little from an interest deduction, so the tax shield is worth less to a REIT. In practice REITs carry no more, and often less, leverage than REOCs.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A REIT reports net income of $40 million, after charging real estate depreciation and amortisation of $25 million. During the year it recognised gains on sales of properties of $6 million, spent $9 million on recurring maintenance capital expenditure, and recorded a non-cash straight-line rent adjustment that increased reported revenue by $3 million. The REIT's funds from operations (FFO) is closest to:

options.C: $47 million.
options.A: $59 million.
options.B: $65 million.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 221 | Alternative Investments

explanations.C: Incorrect. $47 million is adjusted funds from operations: FFO of $59 million less the $9 million of recurring maintenance capital expenditure and the $3 million non-cash straight-line rent accrual. AFFO is a refinement of FFO, not FFO itself.
explanations.A: Correct. FFO begins with net income, adds back real estate depreciation and amortisation as a non-cash charge, and removes gains and losses on property sales as non-recurring: $40 million + $25 million - $6 million = $59 million.
explanations.B: Incorrect. $65 million adds back depreciation but leaves the $6 million of property sale gains in the figure. FFO strips out sale gains and losses precisely because a REIT cannot repeat them year after year.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: Compared with net income, adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) is generally preferred as a measure of a REIT's dividend-paying capacity most likely because:

options.B: it adds back the non-cash straight-line rent accrual, so the measure reflects the average rent over the whole lease term.
options.C: it excludes gains and losses on property sales and adds back interest expense, isolating the return on the property portfolio.
options.A: it reverses a depreciation charge that overstates economic decline and then deducts recurring maintenance capital expenditure.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 222 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. AFFO does the opposite: the straight-line rent accrual is deducted, because it is revenue recognised in the accounts that no tenant has yet paid in cash and that therefore cannot fund a dividend.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Removing gains and losses on sales is a feature of FFO, but interest expense is a genuine cash cost of the REIT's capital structure and is never added back in either FFO or AFFO. Adding it back would describe something closer to EBITDA.
explanations.A: Correct. Real estate depreciation is a large non-cash charge on assets that frequently hold or increase in value, so net income understates distributable cash. AFFO reverses it and then subtracts the recurring capital spending and non-cash rent accruals needed to sustain that cash flow, which is why it tracks sustainable dividends better than either net income or FFO.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A REIT's forward 12-month cash net operating income from its operating properties is $30 million, and the appropriate capitalisation rate for those properties is 6.0%. The REIT also holds cash of $15 million, receivables of $5 million, and land held for development with a market value of $20 million. Its debt is $220 million, other liabilities are $20 million, and 25 million shares are outstanding. Net asset value per share is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 223 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. $11.20 omits the $20 million of land held for development. Non-income-producing assets carried at market value are added to the capitalised value of the operating portfolio precisely because capitalising current net operating income captures none of their worth.
explanations.C: Correct. Capitalising cash net operating income gives $30 million / 0.06 = $500 million for the operating properties. Adding cash, receivables and development land ($40 million) and deducting debt and other liabilities ($240 million) leaves net asset value of $300 million, or $12.00 across 25 million shares.
explanations.A: Incorrect. $20.00 is the gross value of the operating properties per share. Net asset value is a net figure, so all liabilities, and the $220 million of debt in particular, must be subtracted before dividing by shares outstanding.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A buyout fund has committed capital of $100 million, all of which has been drawn. Over its life the fund distributes $150 million in total. Limited partners first receive their contributed capital plus a cumulative preferred return of $8 million; the general partner then receives 100% of further distributions as a catch-up until it has received 20% of the profits distributed; any remainder is split 80/20 between limited partners and the general partner. The general partner's total carried interest is closest to:

options.A: $2.0 million.
options.B: $8.4 million.
options.C: $10.0 million.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 224 | Alternative Investments

explanations.A: Incorrect. $2.0 million is only the catch-up tranche, the amount x that satisfies x = 0.20 x ($8 million + x). Once the catch-up is complete the general partner still takes 20% of everything distributed beyond it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. $8.4 million is 20% of the $42 million of profit left after the $8 million preferred return, which is the answer under a hard hurdle with no catch-up. A catch-up provision exists precisely to put the preferred return back into the profit base.
explanations.C: Correct. Total profit is $150 million - $100 million = $50 million. The catch-up is $2 million and the 80/20 split of the remaining $40 million adds $8 million, giving $10 million. That is the effect of a full catch-up: the general partner ends with 20% of all profit, not only of profit above the hurdle.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A clawback provision in a private equity fund's partnership agreement is best described as an obligation that:

options.C: entitles the general partner to all distributions above the hurdle until it has earned its full percentage of the fund's profits.
options.A: changes the base on which the general partner charges its fee from committed capital to invested capital or net asset value.
options.B: requires the general partner to return carried interest already received when later losses leave it with more than its agreed share.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 225 | Alternative Investments

explanations.C: Incorrect. That describes the catch-up, which works in the general partner's favour and applies before any clawback could arise. The two are easily confused because both adjust the split once the preferred return has been paid.
explanations.A: Incorrect. That describes the customary step-down in the management fee base at the end of the investment period. It is a fee term rather than a profit-sharing correction, and it is why fees on a mature fund fall even though committed capital is unchanged.
explanations.B: Correct. Because carried interest is often paid deal by deal as exits occur, strong early realisations can pay the general partner more than its lifetime 20% once later write-downs are taken. The clawback compels repayment of the excess so that the agreed split holds over the whole life of the fund.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A venture capital firm is considering a $5 million investment in a start-up. It expects the company to be sold for $45 million at the end of three years and requires a return of 50% per year on the investment. Using the venture capital method, the ownership fraction the firm must receive at the time of the investment is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 226 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. 11.1% is $5 million divided by the undiscounted $45 million exit value. That would be the required stake only if the firm demanded no return at all over the three years.
explanations.C: Correct. The post-money valuation is the discounted exit value, $45 million / 1.50^3 = $45 million / 3.375 = $13.33 million. The ownership fraction is the investment divided by the post-money valuation, $5 million / $13.33 million = 37.5%, and the pre-money valuation is the residual $8.33 million.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 60.0% divides the $5 million investment by the pre-money valuation of $8.33 million. Ownership is always measured against the post-money valuation, which already includes the cash the investor is putting in.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A buyout fund acquires a company with EBITDA of $50 million at an enterprise value of 8.0 times EBITDA, funding $240 million of the purchase price with debt. Five years later it sells the company when EBITDA is $70 million, at an exit multiple of 9.0 times EBITDA, with $150 million of debt still outstanding. The multiple of invested capital earned on the equity is closest to:

options.B: 2.4 times.
options.C: 2.6 times.
options.A: 3.0 times.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 227 | Alternative Investments

explanations.B: Incorrect. About 2.4 times results from leaving debt at its $240 million entry level and ignoring the $90 million repaid out of operating cash flow. Debt reduction is one of the three sources of buyout equity return and is often the most dependable.
explanations.C: Incorrect. About 2.6 times results from exiting at the 8.0 times entry multiple, which removes the multiple expansion. Expansion of the exit multiple is the least controllable driver, which is why sponsors are reluctant to underwrite a deal that depends on it.
explanations.A: Correct. Equity invested is $400 million - $240 million = $160 million and equity realised is (9.0 x $70 million) - $150 million = $480 million, so the multiple of invested capital is 3.0 times. It decomposes into EBITDA growth, multiple expansion and debt reduction; measured at the deal level it is gross of fund fees and carry, so the net multiple limited partners report will be lower.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A fully collateralised long position in a commodity futures contract is rolled each month. At the roll date the expiring near-month contract is priced at $50.00 and the next-month contract into which the position is rolled is priced at $51.50. The roll return realised on this roll is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 228 | Alternative Investments

explanations.A: Correct. Roll return is the near-month price less the farther-month price divided by the near-month price: ($50.00 - $51.50) / $50.00 = -3.0%. The deferred contract is dearer, so the market is in contango and a long roller sells low and buys high, producing a negative roll return that drags on total return.
explanations.B: Incorrect. -2.9% divides the $1.50 roll cost by the $51.50 deferred price. The convention measures the roll against the price of the near contract being sold, which is the position actually given up.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A roll return of +3.0% would require the deferred contract to trade below the expiring one, that is, a market in backwardation. Here the curve slopes upward, so the sign must be negative.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: A commodity is in short supply and market inventories have fallen to unusually low levels. This situation is most likely to be associated with:

options.C: a high cost of carry, which under the theory of storage tends to push the futures curve into contango.
options.A: a high convenience yield, which under the theory of storage tends to push the futures curve into backwardation.
options.B: heavy hedging by producers, which under the insurance theory lifts futures prices above the expected future spot price.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 229 | Alternative Investments

explanations.C: Incorrect. High storage and financing costs do push a curve into contango, but that describes a market with ample inventory, where holders must be compensated for storing surplus material rather than rewarded for having any at all.
explanations.A: Correct. The theory of storage prices a futures contract as spot plus storage and financing costs less the convenience yield, the non-monetary benefit of holding physical inventory. When stocks are scarce that benefit is large enough to outweigh the cost of carry, the net cost of carry turns negative, and the curve inverts into backwardation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heavy producer hedging is the insurance or hedging pressure argument, but it works in the opposite direction: short hedgers must pay long speculators to bear the risk, so futures are priced below the expected future spot price, not above it.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: The total return on a fully collateralised long position in a commodity futures index will most likely differ from the change in the spot prices of the underlying commodities because:

options.C: futures prices converge to the spot price at expiration, so any difference can only reflect storage costs embedded in the spot price.
options.A: the index also earns a collateral return on the posted cash and a roll return that depends on the shape of the futures curve.
options.B: the index is computed as an excess-return series, which strips out the spot price change and captures only the change in the basis.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 230 | Alternative Investments

explanations.C: Incorrect. Convergence holds for a single contract carried to expiration, but an index position never takes delivery: it rolls into a later contract, and that roll is where most of the divergence from spot arises.
explanations.A: Correct. The total return on a collateralised futures index is the sum of three components: the spot return, the roll return earned or paid each time the position moves along the term structure, and the collateral return on the cash backing the notional exposure. Only the first tracks spot appreciation, so a persistent contango can leave index returns well below the rise in spot prices.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An excess-return index does exclude the collateral return, but it still contains both the spot and the roll components. In any case the question concerns the total-return series, which adds the interest earned on collateral back in.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: Reported returns on a broad index of hedge funds are most likely biased upward relative to the return actually earned by the average hedge fund investor because:

options.A: the constituents are equally weighted rather than asset-weighted, so the largest funds are underrepresented in the reported average.
options.B: index returns are reported net of the extra layer of management and incentive fees that funds of funds charge above the manager fees.
options.C: funds that close after poor results leave the index, while a new entrant's favourable earlier record is backfilled into the history.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 231 | Alternative Investments

explanations.A: Incorrect. Equal weighting changes which funds dominate the average but does not push it systematically upward, and many hedge fund indices are equally weighted by design rather than by oversight.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A second layer of fund-of-funds fees reduces reported returns rather than inflating them. Fund-of-funds indices are in fact sometimes preferred as a benchmark because they reflect fees an investor actually pays and are less exposed to backfill.
explanations.C: Correct. Survivorship bias removes the record of managers who shut down after losses, and backfill or instant-history bias adds an incubated fund's flattering past once it begins reporting. Both admit good records and drop bad ones, so the index overstates what an investor holding the whole universe would have earned; voluntary self-selection in reporting works the same way.

subject: Alternative Investments

stem: An ETF is trading at a price above the value of the securities in its underlying basket. The feature of the ETF structure that is most likely to close that gap is:

options.C: authorised participants delivering the basket and selling the new shares.
options.A: the fund manager redeeming investors' shares directly at the day's NAV.
options.B: the exchange obliging market makers to quote within a band around NAV.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 232 | Portfolio Management

explanations.C: Correct. When the ETF is rich to its basket, an authorised participant buys the underlying securities, delivers them to the fund for a creation unit, and sells those shares in the market. Buying the basket and selling ETF shares pushes the two values together, and the arbitrage keeps working because creation units are available on demand.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Direct redemption at net asset value is the open-end mutual fund mechanism. ETF investors sell on the exchange to other investors; only authorised participants deal with the fund itself, and they do so in large creation units, usually in kind.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Exchanges can designate liquidity providers with quoting obligations, but those obligations are framed in terms of maximum spread and minimum size, not a band around net asset value. It is the arbitrage profit, not a quoting rule, that anchors price to value.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: The role of an authorised participant in the exchange-traded fund market is best described as:

options.B: an agent that calculates and publishes the intraday indicative value.
options.C: a broker-dealer entitled to exchange security baskets for creation units.
options.A: a dealer contractually bound to buy investor shares back at fund NAV.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 233 | Portfolio Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. The intraday indicative value is computed and disseminated by the exchange or a calculation agent. It is a reference number for traders during the session, and producing it confers no ability to create or redeem fund shares.
explanations.C: Correct. The authorised participant has a contractual right to transact in the primary market with the fund, delivering or receiving a specified basket in exchange for or in return for creation units. That primary-market access is exactly what allows it to arbitrage a gap between price and net asset value.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No party stands ready to buy investor shares at net asset value. Investors transact with other investors on the exchange at market prices, which is the reason an ETF can trade at a premium or a discount at all.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: Which of the following is most likely a source of tracking error for an index-tracking ETF?

options.A: A buyer on the exchange pays half of the quoted bid-ask spread on entry.
options.B: The fund lends portfolio securities and credits the fee income to it.
options.C: The fund holds a representative sample rather than every constituent.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 234 | Portfolio Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. Half the spread is a cost borne by the individual investor in the secondary market. It affects that investor's realised return rather than the fund's net asset value return, so it belongs to total cost of ownership rather than to tracking error.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Securities lending revenue returned to the fund offsets expenses and normally narrows the gap between fund and index returns. Its real drawback is counterparty and collateral risk should the borrower fail, not additional tracking error.
explanations.C: Correct. Tracking error compares the fund's net asset value return with the index return. Sampled or optimised replication leaves the fund holding something other than the index, so its return diverges, along with the drag from fees, uninvested cash, and the timing of index reconstitutions.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A premium of an ETF's market price over its net asset value is most likely to persist when:

options.C: the underlying securities trade in a market closed while the ETF trades.
options.A: the ETF's spread is narrow and its secondary market turnover is heavy.
options.B: several authorised participants compete to create shares in the primary market.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 235 | Portfolio Management

explanations.C: Correct. Persistent deviations arise when arbitrage is impeded. If the underlying market is closed, the published net asset value is stale while the ETF price reflects newer information, so the apparent premium cannot be arbitraged. The same effect appears when creations are capped or the basket is illiquid and costly to assemble.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A narrow spread and heavy turnover indicate an efficient secondary market, which is precisely the condition under which price tracks net asset value closely. Those are indicators of low trading cost, not of a persistent premium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Competition among authorised participants is the force that removes a premium, since each of them profits by creating shares while the ETF is rich. More competitors means the gap closes faster, not that it persists.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: An investor who intends to hold an ETF position for several years is comparing total cost of ownership across funds. The cost component that most likely dominates over that horizon is:

options.A: the bid-ask spread, since it is incurred on both the entry and the exit.
options.B: the management fee, since it is charged for every year of the holding.
options.C: the premium or discount, since it moves throughout each trading session.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 236 | Portfolio Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. The spread is a one-off cost at each side of the trade. It is the dominant component for a short-horizon or frequently traded position, which is why a tactical investor may accept a higher fee in exchange for a tighter market.
explanations.B: Correct. Total cost of ownership divides into one-off trading costs and recurring holding costs. Trading costs are paid twice whatever the horizon, so as the holding period lengthens the recurring fee and the tracking difference come to dominate the comparison between two similar funds.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A premium or discount matters only through the difference between the level at purchase and the level at sale, and over a long holding it is neither recurring nor predictable in sign. It is a trading-cost item rather than a holding-cost item.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: Compared with a physically replicating ETF, an investor in a synthetic ETF that obtains its index exposure through a total return swap most likely bears additional:

options.B: liquidity risk, since swap-based funds cannot be redeemed by participants.
options.C: tracking error, since a swap cannot deliver the index return net of fees.
options.A: counterparty risk, since the return depends on the swap provider paying.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 237 | Portfolio Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. Synthetic ETFs still operate a creation and redemption process, usually settled in cash rather than in kind. Their secondary-market liquidity rests on the same primary-market arbitrage as any other ETF.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A swap is normally written to pay the index return less an agreed fee, so synthetic replication typically produces lower tracking error than physical sampling. Reduced tracking error is the main reason such structures are used for hard-to-access indexes.
explanations.A: Correct. In a swap-based structure the fund holds collateral and contracts with a counterparty to receive the index return. If that counterparty fails, the fund is left with the collateral and an unpaid claim, so credit exposure to the swap provider is an explicit added risk that collateral and frequent resets limit but do not remove.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: Which of the following is an assumption of arbitrage pricing theory?

options.A: Asset returns are generated by a model with a limited number of factors.
options.B: The market portfolio is mean-variance efficient and held by all investors.
options.C: Investor utility is quadratic, so only mean and variance affect choices.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 238 | Portfolio Management

explanations.A: Correct. Arbitrage pricing theory rests on three assumptions: a factor model describes asset returns, there are enough assets that asset-specific risk can be diversified away, and no arbitrage opportunity exists among well-diversified portfolios. It never needs the market portfolio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That is the central assumption of the capital asset pricing model, which is what forces the CAPM down to a single market factor. Arbitrage pricing theory is deliberately agnostic about the number and the identity of the factors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Quadratic utility, or alternatively normally distributed returns, is one route to justifying mean-variance analysis. Arbitrage pricing theory is a no-arbitrage argument and requires no particular utility function.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: Compared with a macroeconomic factor model, the factor sensitivities in a fundamental factor model are most likely:

options.B: estimated as slopes on factor surprises, with factor returns given already.
options.C: specified in advance from firm attributes, with factor returns estimated.
options.A: constrained to equal one, so that only the intercept has to be estimated.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 239 | Portfolio Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. That describes the macroeconomic factor model. There the factors are surprises in observable series such as inflation or industrial production, and each asset's sensitivity is the slope estimated from a time-series regression of its return on those surprises.
explanations.C: Correct. In a fundamental model the sensitivity is an observable and usually standardised attribute of the company, such as its book-to-price or its size expressed in standard deviations from the universe mean. The betas are therefore inputs, and a cross-sectional regression backs out the factor returns.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No standard factor model fixes every sensitivity at one. A sensitivity of one to a single factor and zero to all the others describes a factor portfolio, which is built from a model rather than being an assumption inside one.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A statistical factor model is best described as a model in which the factors are:

options.B: observable company attributes such as size and the book-to-market ratio.
options.C: published macroeconomic series such as inflation and industrial production.
options.A: portfolios derived from the historical covariance of the returns themselves.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 240 | Portfolio Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. Factors defined by company attributes define a fundamental factor model. There the standardised attribute itself is the sensitivity, and the factor returns are what the cross-sectional regression estimates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Factors taken from published economic series define a macroeconomic factor model. There the factor is the surprise component of the series, and each asset's sensitivity to it is estimated by time-series regression.
explanations.A: Correct. A statistical model applies factor analysis or principal components to a matrix of historical returns and extracts the combinations that explain the most covariance. Because the factors emerge from the data, they need not correspond to anything economically interpretable and they can be unstable out of sample.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A portfolio's active return for a period was 1.50%. Its active exposure to the value factor was +0.30 and that factor returned 4.00%; its active exposure to the size factor was -0.20 and that factor returned 3.00%. The portion of active return attributable to security selection is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 241 | Portfolio Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.60% is the part of the active return explained by the two factor bets, so it is the factor return contribution rather than the selection contribution. Security selection is what is left after the factor bets are stripped out.
explanations.B: Correct. The factor contribution is the sum of each active exposure times its factor return: (0.30 x 4.00%) + (-0.20 x 3.00%) = 1.20% - 0.60% = 0.60%. Security selection is the residual that the factor model cannot account for, 1.50% - 0.60% = 0.90%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 2.10% adds the 0.60% factor contribution to the 1.50% active return instead of removing it. The decomposition is additive, so the two components must sum to the active return, not exceed it.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A risk model attributes a portfolio's active risk to an active factor variance of 16 and an active specific variance of 9, both measured in percent squared. The portfolio's active risk is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 242 | Portfolio Management

explanations.C: Correct. Active risk squared is the sum of the active factor variance and the active specific variance, so total active variance is 16 + 9 = 25 and active risk is its square root, 5.00%. The variances add because the model treats specific risk as uncorrelated with factor risk.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 7.00% adds the two standard deviations, 4% plus 3%. Standard deviations of uncorrelated components do not add, their squares do, which is why the total is smaller than the sum of the parts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 12.50% is half of the active variance and is not a risk measure at all. Variance is expressed in percent squared and must be square-rooted before it can be compared with a return.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A factor portfolio constructed from a multifactor model is best described as a portfolio with:

options.C: unit sensitivity to one factor and zero sensitivity to every other factor.
options.A: factor sensitivities matched to those of a designated benchmark index.
options.B: the largest expected return available at a given level of total variance.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 243 | Portfolio Management

explanations.C: Correct. A factor portfolio isolates one source of risk: it is built to have a sensitivity of one to the target factor and zero to all the others. That makes it the pure instrument for adding or hedging a single exposure without disturbing the rest of the risk profile.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Matching a benchmark's factor sensitivities describes a tracking portfolio, which is constructed to reproduce the benchmark's exposures as a whole rather than to isolate one factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That describes a portfolio on the mean-variance efficient frontier. Efficiency is defined over total risk and expected return, whereas a factor portfolio is defined purely by its exposure profile.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A $25 million portfolio has an expected monthly return of 1.0% and a monthly standard deviation of 4.0%. Returns are assumed to be normally distributed and the critical z-value for the 5% tail is 1.65. Using the parametric method, the 5% monthly VaR is closest to:
origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 244 | Portfolio Management

explanations.A: Correct. The 5th percentile monthly return is 1.0% - (1.65 x 4.0%) = -5.6%. Applied to $25 million that is a loss of $1,400,000, so the portfolio is expected to lose at least that amount in 5% of months.
explanations.B: Incorrect. $1,650,000 is 1.65 x 4.0% x $25 million, which leaves the expected return out of the calculation. Dropping the mean is a common shortcut for a one-day horizon where it is negligible, but over a month a positive expected return reduces the loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. $1,900,000 adds the expected return to the tail rather than subtracting it, giving (1.0% + 6.6%) x $25 million. A positive expected return makes the percentile loss smaller, not larger.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: A portfolio has a one-day 5% value at risk of $2 million. This is best interpreted as:

options.B: an average loss of $2 million across the worst 5% of trading days.
options.C: a 5% chance the portfolio loses $2 million or more on a given day.
options.A: the largest one-day loss the portfolio can suffer outside a crisis.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 245 | Portfolio Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. The average loss conditional on exceeding the threshold is conditional VaR, also called expected shortfall. It is always at least as large as VaR, and it exists precisely because VaR is silent about the size of tail losses.
explanations.C: Correct. Value at risk is a quantile of the loss distribution: it states the minimum loss expected to occur with the stated frequency over the stated horizon. It says nothing at all about how much larger the loss might be once the threshold is breached.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Value at risk is not a maximum loss. Reading it as one is the best-known misuse of the measure, since the whole meaning of the 5% is that larger losses should be expected on roughly one day in twenty.

subject: Portfolio Management

stem: Compared with Monte Carlo simulation, estimating value at risk by historical simulation most likely:

options.A: lets the analyst change one correlation while holding others fixed.
options.B: generates outcomes more extreme than the sample period contained.
options.C: needs no assumption about the shape of the return distribution.

origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 246 | Portfolio Management
